title: Britain's Tallest Stone Row: Ancient Builders Hauled 25-Tonne Stones 11 Miles
summary:
The Devil's Arrows are three massive standing stones in northern England, rising as high as seven meters (23 feet). They form Britain's tallest surviving prehistoric stone row. But for centuries, no one knew where the stones came from.

A new study led by Curtin University, in collaboration with the University of York, has pinpointed the source: Brimham Rocks, a rugged area in North Yorkshire — at least 18 kilometers (11 miles) away.

That's much farther than previously thought. Earlier research had suggested Plumpton Rocks, which is closer, as the likely source. But the new evidence points to Brimham.

"Our research shows these stones weren't simply taken from the nearest available source — they were deliberately chosen from a challenging landscape 18 kilometers away," said lead author Dr. Anthony Clarke.

To figure this out, the team used a new low-impact sampling technique. They pressed adhesive tape onto the stones to collect tiny mineral grains — without damaging the monument. Then they analyzed the age "fingerprints" of those grains and compared them with geological samples from possible source sites. The match was clear.

The evidence also ruled out natural explanations like glacial movement. That means people intentionally moved these enormous stones.

Each stone weighs more than 25 tonnes. Moving them would have required incredible planning, coordination, and engineering skill. The choice of source suggests the landscape around Brimham Rocks held cultural, symbolic, or spiritual meaning.

"These results show that ancient communities were making deliberate and meaningful choices about where their stones came from," said co-author Dr. Jim Leary.

The team now plans to use their non-invasive technique on other standing stones and to carry out targeted excavations at both the Devil's Arrows and Brimham Rocks.
why_it_matters: It shows that prehistoric communities could organise large-scale projects and shared beliefs, which challenges the old idea that ancient people simply grabbed whatever stone was closest.

background_read: Britain is dotted with prehistoric monuments. The most famous is Stonehenge, a circle of huge stones on Salisbury Plain in southern England. Its smaller "bluestones" were traced to the Preseli Hills in Wales, hundreds of kilometres away — proof that ancient people sometimes moved stones long distances on purpose.
The Devil's Arrows are three enormous stones standing in a line just outside the town of Boroughbridge in North Yorkshire.

Brimham Rocks, the source identified in the new study, is a real landscape of strangely balanced gritstone formations in North Yorkshire. It is now looked after by the National Trust, a charity that cares for historic and natural sites in England, Wales and Northern Ireland.
Curtin University is a large public university in Perth, Australia, and the University of York is a research university in the north of England. Both work on archaeology and geology.

Geologists identify a stone's origin by studying the minerals and ages inside it, because every rock source has its own "fingerprint". Modern archaeology often tries to study protected monuments without digging, using non-invasive techniques like the tape sampling described here.

perspectives.description: The study rebuilds a 4,000-year-old decision: people chose a difficult, distant source on purpose. It also demonstrates a low-impact sampling method that can be reused on fragile monuments, so many more sites can be studied without damaging them.

Some researchers will argue that the tape method only samples the stone's surface, which weathers over thousands of years, and that a stronger match would require excavation. Others point out that earlier work favoured Plumpton Rocks, so the case may not be closed yet.

Stonehenge's bluestones were also hauled from far away, so this fits a broader pattern: in prehistoric Britain, the place a stone came from could matter more than how easy it was to fetch. That suggests monuments were about meaning and belief, not just convenience.

The team plans to run the same technique on other standing stones and to excavate at both the Devil's Arrows and Brimham Rocks. If more monuments turn out to use distant sources, textbooks may need to describe prehistoric Britain as far more connected and organised than once thought.
